title: Solomon's knot — elongated chain with a lock stitch
subtitle: The mesh backbone of open-weave shawls and bags
excerpt: Solomon's knot is an elongated chain loop locked in place by a double crochet into its back bar. The result is a long, knotted mesh element used to build open-weave fabric for shawls, market bags, and lace wrap panels. It produces a distinctive large-holed net that's too open for standard stitch patterns but exactly right for its purpose.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776 — the Solomon's knot stitch in hairpin and open-mesh lace work. Weldon's Practical Crochet, Vol. 6 (1891) — Solomon's knot mesh for filet-style borders.

glossaryTerms.definition: An elongated chain loop, stretched to 1-2 cm, with a dc worked into its single back bar to lock it in place. A pair of Solomon's knots with a dc between them is the repeating unit of open Solomon's knot mesh. Also called lover's knot or crazy knot.

content.text: is one of the oldest crochet lace stitches — a loop stretched long and pinned in place with a dc before moving on. Unlike other stitches, there is no row of foundation chain to work into. The knots build on each other to form a large-holed mesh that is simultaneously open and structural. Used for market bags it holds shape under weight; in shawls the large holes create a dramatic lace drape.
Draw up the loop on the hook to about 1-2 cm — much longer than a normal chain stitch.
Yarn over and pull through the extended loop to chain it off (1 elongated chain made).
Identify the single back bar of this elongated chain — it runs along the back of the long loop. Insert the hook under this single back bar only.
Yarn over and draw up a loop (2 loops on hook). Yarn over, draw through both loops — one dc made. This locks the knot.
Make a foundation row of Solomon's knots — pairs of knots separated by dc anchors.
Turn. Make 2 Solomon's knots (turning knots). Skip the first knot of the foundation row.
Work a dc into the dc between the first and second knot of the row below. *Make 2 Solomon's knots, dc into the next between-knot dc. Repeat from *.

items.symptom: Can't find the back bar for the locking dc
items.cause: Holding the elongated loop too tightly, closing the loop before the back bar is visible
items.fix: After making the elongated chain, hold it flat and slightly taut between thumb and forefinger. The back bar is the single strand running along the back side of the loop — it becomes visible when the loop is held open.

items.cause: Inconsistent loop extension when drawing up the elongated chain
items.fix: Practice extending the loop to the same length each time. Many crocheters use a finger as a size guide — wrap the extended loop once around a finger to calibrate a consistent 1.5 cm length.

content.text: Picot chain is a similar open-mesh edging technique — smaller and lighter than Solomon's knot mesh. For structured open mesh at a larger scale, filet crochet (dc and ch-2 mesh on a grid) gives more control over the pattern layout.
